key_insight: A review-based observational model can estimate how often conference decisions would flip under a different reviewer set, revealing substantial peer-review noise in ICLR 2017-2025.
engineering_relevance: The study gives conference organizers and ML systems researchers a practical, data-driven way to quantify decision stability without running an expensive second committee.
method: Bayesian ordered-probit model separates paper quality from reviewer noise.
Logistic decision model maps review scores to accept/reject outcomes.
Monte Carlo simulation of two independent committees estimates disagreement rates for k=2,3,4 reviewers.
evidence_signal: Calibrated on 36,113 papers and 134,912 reviews, the estimator matched NeurIPS 2021 and internal 2+2 reviewer splits, with estimated disagreement around 23.3% at k=3 and accepted-paper flip rates of 30-50%.
watch_item: The LLM-era breakpoint test has very low power, and the absence of post-2022 review text/confidence data limits causal attribution.
paper_title: The Review Lottery: Calibrating an Observational Estimator of Peer-Review Noise (ICLR 2017-2025)
